description: Congee with Century Egg is a quintessential Chinese comfort food, a warm and savory rice porridge perfect for breakfast or a light meal. This creamy congee, infused with the unique flavor of century eggs and often complemented by shredded pork, offers a delightful balance of textures and tastes. It's a nourishing and deeply satisfying dish that embodies the heart of traditional Chinese home cooking.

ingredients.item: Pork loin or lean pork shoulder

ingredients.notes: chopped, white and green parts separated

instructions.title: Prepare the Rice
instructions.text: Wash jasmine rice thoroughly under cold running water until the water runs clear. Soak the rice in water for at least 30 minutes, or preferably overnight, to shorten cooking time and achieve a creamier texture. Drain well before cooking.

instructions.title: Marinate the Pork
instructions.text: Slice the pork loin into thin strips or small cubes. In a small bowl, marinate the pork with a pinch of salt, a dash of white pepper, 1 teaspoon of cooking oil, and 1 teaspoon of cornstarch (if using). Mix well and let it sit for at least 15 minutes.

instructions.title: Prepare Century Eggs and Aromatics
instructions.text: Carefully peel the century eggs and rinse them. Cut two of the century eggs into small wedges or cubes for the congee, and reserve the third one to slice for garnish. Finely julienne the fresh ginger and chop the green onions, separating the white parts from the green parts.

instructions.title: Start the Congee Base
instructions.text: In a large heavy-bottomed pot, combine the soaked and drained rice with 10 cups of water or chicken broth. Bring the mixture to a rolling boil over high heat, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover the pot, and simmer for 30 minutes, stirring every 5-10 minutes.

instructions.title: Add Pork and Century Eggs
instructions.text: After 30 minutes, the rice should have started to break down and become thicker. Add the marinated pork and the diced century egg pieces (from two eggs) to the congee. Continue to simmer for another 10-15 minutes, stirring frequently, until the pork is cooked through and the congee reaches your desired creamy, porridge-like consistency.

instructions.title: Season and Serve
instructions.text: Season the congee with salt and white pepper to taste. Stir in the white parts of the chopped green onions and the sesame oil. Ladle the hot congee into individual serving bowls. Garnish each bowl with the reserved sliced century egg, fresh ginger juliennes, and the green parts of the green onions. Serve immediately, perhaps with a side of crispy fried dough (youtiao).

tips: For an extra creamy congee, freeze the washed rice overnight before cooking. The freezing and thawing process breaks down the rice grains, making them cook faster and achieve a smoother texture.
Don't overcrowd the pot when adding the pork; add it in batches if necessary to maintain the congee's temperature and prevent the pork from clumping together.
Congee thickens as it cools. If reheating, you may need to add a little hot water or broth to achieve the desired consistency, stirring well over low heat.
article:
Embrace the comforting embrace of a warm bowl of congee, a beloved staple in Chinese cuisine that offers nourishment and gentle flavors. While plain congee is a canvas for many toppings, one of the most iconic and surprisingly delicious variations is Congee with Century Egg, often enhanced with lean pork. This classic Chinese breakfast recipe is more than just a meal; it's a culinary journey into tradition, offering a unique blend of textures and umami that has captivated palates for centuries. If you're looking to expand your breakfast horizons beyond toast and cereal, diving into the world of Century Egg Congee is an adventure worth taking.

## What is Century Egg Congee?
At its heart, congee is a type of rice porridge, made by simmering rice in a large amount of water or broth until the grains break down into a creamy, soupy consistency. It’s a versatile dish, often served for breakfast, as a light meal, or even for those feeling under the weather due to its easy digestibility.

The star of this particular congee variation is the century egg, also known as pidan or preserved egg. Don't let its striking appearance—a dark, gelatinous albumen and a creamy, dark green yolk—intimidate you. These eggs, typically duck, chicken, or quail eggs, are preserved in a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime, and rice hulls for several weeks to months. The preservation process transforms the egg, giving it a unique, savory, slightly pungent, and deeply umami flavor that is surprisingly mild once you acquire the taste. When diced and stirred into hot congee, the century egg imparts a distinctive richness and a slightly firm, yet yielding texture that complements the soft rice beautifully. Often, this dish is further elevated by adding shredded lean pork, which provides a savory counterpoint and additional depth of flavor, making for a truly satisfying Century Egg Congee.

## Ingredients You'll Need
Creating a delicious bowl of Century Egg Congee doesn't require an extensive list of ingredients, but quality and freshness certainly make a difference.

*   **Rice:** 1 cup long-grain jasmine rice or short-grain rice. Jasmine rice is preferred for its aroma and ability to break down into a creamy texture.
*   **Water or Broth:** 8-10 cups of water or chicken broth. Broth will add significantly more flavor.
*   **Century Eggs:** 2-3 century eggs, peeled and diced.
*   **Lean Pork (optional):** 4-6 oz lean pork loin or shoulder, thinly sliced or shredded.
*   **Ginger:** 1-inch piece, peeled and thinly sliced or julienned.
*   **Scallions:** 2-3 stalks, chopped for garnish.
*   **Seasoning:** Salt, white pepper, and a drizzle of sesame oil to taste.
*   **Marinade for Pork (if using):** 1 tsp soy sauce, 1/2 tsp cornstarch, a pinch of white pepper.

## How to Make Century Egg Congee (Step-by-Step)
Making perfect Century Egg Congee is a process of patience and gentle simmering.

1.  **Prepare the Rice:** Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold water until the water runs clear. For an even creamier congee, soak the rice in water for at least 30 minutes, or even overnight. This helps the grains break down faster.
2.  **Marinate the Pork (if using):** If using pork, combine the thinly sliced or shredded pork with soy sauce, cornstarch, and white pepper. Mix well and set aside for at least 15 minutes. The cornstarch helps tenderize the pork and keeps it moist.
3.  **Start the Congee Base:** In a large, heavy-bottomed pot, combine the rinsed rice and 8-10 cups of water or broth. Bring to a boil over high heat. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover the pot partially (leaving a small gap for steam to escape), and simmer for at least 1.5 to 2 hours. Stir occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom. The goal is for the rice grains to completely break down and form a thick, creamy porridge.
4.  **Add Century Eggs and Pork:** After the congee has been simmering for about 1.5 hours and has reached a creamy consistency, add the diced century eggs and marinated pork (if using). Stir them into the congee.
5.  **Continue Simmering:** Continue to simmer for another 15-20 minutes, or until the pork is cooked through and the flavors have melded. If the congee becomes too thick, you can add a little more hot water or broth to reach your desired consistency.
6.  **Season and Garnish:** Season the congee with salt and white pepper to taste. Ladle the hot Century Egg Congee into bowls, garnish with fresh chopped scallions, and drizzle with a few drops of sesame oil just before serving.

## Tips for the Perfect Congee
Achieving that silky, comforting texture in your congee is easier with a few key tips:

*   **Soak Your Rice:** As mentioned, soaking the rice significantly reduces cooking time and helps the grains break down more evenly, resulting in a creamier texture.
*   **Use a Heavy Pot:** A heavy-bottomed pot distributes heat more evenly and reduces the chances of the congee sticking and burning at the bottom.
*   **Don't Skimp on Liquid:** Congee requires a lot of liquid. Start with a 1:8 or 1:10 rice-to-liquid ratio. You can always add more hot liquid if it gets too thick.
*   **Stir Occasionally:** While the congee simmers, give it a stir every 15-20 minutes, especially towards the end, to prevent sticking and ensure even cooking.
*   **Adjust Consistency:** The ideal congee consistency is a matter of personal preference. Some prefer it thicker, almost like a gruel, while others like it looser and soupier. Adjust by adding more hot water/broth or simmering longer.
*   **Season at the End:** Add salt and pepper towards the end of cooking. If you season too early, the salt can concentrate as the liquid reduces, making it overly salty.

## Serving Suggestions & Pairings
Century Egg Congee is a complete meal in itself, but it truly shines when paired with traditional Chinese breakfast accompaniments.

*   **Youtiao (Chinese Fried Dough Sticks):** The undisputed champion pairing. These crispy, airy fried dough sticks are perfect for dipping into the hot congee, absorbing its savory flavors and adding a delightful textural contrast.
*   **Pickled Vegetables:** A small plate of pickled radish, cucumber, or mustard greens offers a refreshing, tangy crunch that cuts through the richness of the congee.
*   **Soy Sauce and Chili Oil:** For those who like an extra kick, a dash of light soy sauce or a spoonful of homemade chili oil can elevate the flavors.
*   **Other Dim Sum Items:** If you're hosting a larger breakfast, consider serving your congee alongside other popular dim sum items like steamed buns (baozi), spring rolls, or shrimp dumplings (har gow).
*   **White Pepper:** A final sprinkle of white pepper just before eating enhances the aroma and adds a subtle warmth.

## Variations and Add-ins
While Century Egg Congee is a classic, the beauty of congee lies in its adaptability. Don't hesitate to experiment!

*   **Different Meats:** Instead of pork, try shredded chicken, thinly sliced fish, or even ground beef. Ensure meats are cooked through.
*   **Salted Duck Egg:** For another layer of umami and a different texture, add diced salted duck egg along with the century egg. The two eggs complement each other wonderfully.
*   **Vegetables:** Incorporate finely diced carrots, mushrooms (shiitake or oyster), or leafy greens like spinach or bok choy during the last 20 minutes of cooking for added nutrients and color.
*   **Peanuts:** Roasted peanuts added as a garnish provide a crunchy texture and nutty flavor.
*   **Dried Scallops/Shrimp:** For an even deeper seafood umami, add a few rehydrated dried scallops or shrimp to the congee base as it simmers.
*   **Five Spice Powder:** A tiny pinch of five-spice powder can add an aromatic depth, especially if using pork.

## Storage and Reheating
Congee is best enjoyed fresh, but leftovers can be stored and reheated.

*   **Refrigeration:** Store leftover Century Egg Congee in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2-3 days.
*   **Freezing:** While possible, freezing congee can alter its texture, making it a bit more watery or grainy upon reheating. If you choose to freeze, store in freezer-safe containers for up to 1 month.
*   **Reheating:** When reheating congee, it will likely have thickened considerably. Transfer it to a pot and add a splash of water or broth (hot is best) to loosen it back to your desired consistency. Heat gently over low to medium heat, stirring frequently, until heated through. Avoid high heat, which can cause it to stick or burn.

Exploring the world of Chinese breakfast recipes often leads to delightful discoveries, and Century Egg Congee is certainly one of them. Its unique flavor profile, comforting warmth, and incredible versatility make it a dish worth mastering. Whether you're a seasoned chef or a culinary novice, this detailed guide provides everything you need to prepare a truly authentic and satisfying bowl of Century Egg Congee right in your own kitchen. Enjoy the journey into this timeless classic!
